issue.issue_text: Whether an accused acquires an indefeasible right to be released on bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on account of the investigating agency's failure to complete the investigation within the stipulated period.

facts: The appellants were arrested and had been in custody since April 8, 2018.
The statutory 90-day period for completing the investigation was set to expire on July 7, 2018.
Before the expiry, the High Court directed that the investigation be conducted by a senior police officer (ASP rank).
A charge-sheet was filed on July 5, 2018, by an officer of a lower rank, which did not comply with the High Court's order.
Consequently, the Magistrate returned the charge-sheet to the police.
After the 90-day period expired, the appellants applied for bail under Section 167(2) CrPC, arguing that the investigation was not complete within the time limit.
law: Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) mandates that an investigation must be completed within a stipulated period (90 or 60 days, depending on the offense) if the accused is in custody.

The Court affirmed the legal principle, established in cases like *Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra*, that upon the expiry of this period, an "indefeasible right" to be released on bail accrues to the accused.
This right is a direct consequence of the investigating agency's "default" in not completing the investigation on time.
The right is only conditional on the accused being prepared to furnish the bail as directed by the court.
The Court also clarified that the provisions of the CrPC do not empower any court, including the High Court, to extend the statutory period for investigation prescribed under Section 167(2).
application: The Court applied the law to the facts by noting that the 90-day period for investigation ended on July 7, 2018.

As of that date, there was no valid charge-sheet before the Magistrate. The one that had been submitted was returned for non-compliance with a High Court order, meaning the investigation was not legally complete for the purposes of Section 167(2).
The argument that the High Court's order had implicitly extended the time for investigation was rejected, as the law does not permit such an extension.
Therefore, on the 91st day, when the appellants applied for bail, the investigating agency was in default.
This default triggered the appellants' indefeasible right to be released on bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that an accused acquires an indefeasible right to be released on bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC if the investigating agency fails to complete the investigation and file a valid charge-sheet within the prescribed period of 90 or 60 days. Since no valid charge-sheet was on record when the 90-day period expired, the appellants were entitled to be released on bail due to the investigating agency's default.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grant of default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC prohibits the subsequent arrest or re-arrest of the accused on cogent grounds for the same charge.

facts: The accused were granted 'default bail' under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) because the investigating agency failed to complete the investigation within the prescribed 90-day period.
law: Section 167(2) of the CrPC grants an accused an 'indefeasible right' to be released on bail if the investigation is not completed within the stipulated time (60 or 90 days). This is a statutory right based on the default of the investigating agency, not on the merits of the case.
application: The Supreme Court clarified that the grant of default bail is a remedy for the procedural lapse of the investigating agency and does not equate to an acquittal or a final decision on the merits of the charges.
The Court explicitly stated that the grant of default bail "does not prohibit or otherwise prevent the arrest or re-arrest of the petitioner on cogent grounds in respect of the subject charge."

It distinguished between default bail and regular bail. If an accused is re-arrested on cogent grounds (for example, after the charge sheet is filed), they are then entitled to apply for regular bail, which the court will consider on its own merits based on the evidence and circumstances of the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that granting default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC does not prohibit the subsequent arrest or re-arrest of the accused for the same charge, as long as there are cogent grounds for such an action. The right to default bail is not a permanent immunity from custody.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused acquires an indefeasible right to be released on bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on account of the investigating agency's failure to complete the investigation within the stipulated period.
appellant_arguments: As the charge-sheet filed on 05.07.2018 was returned by the Magistrate, there was no valid charge-sheet before the court upon the expiry of the 90-day period.
The Code of Criminal Procedure does not permit any extension of the period for investigation, and the High Court's order could not be interpreted as granting such an extension.
Since the appellants had shown their willingness and filed an application for bail after the statutory period expired, they had acquired an indefeasible right to be released.
respondent_arguments: The investigation was completed and the charge-sheet was filed on 05.07.2018.
The return of the charge-sheet by the Magistrate for compliance with a High Court order should be construed as a step towards further investigation, not as a failure to file within the time limit.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An indefeasible right to bail accrues in favour of an accused person once they have shown their willingness to be admitted to the benefits of bail and have filed an appropriate application for it.
obiter: An accused person should get a fair trial in accordance with the accepted principles of natural justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An accused acquires an indefeasible right to be released on bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure once the statutory period for investigation expires and they have filed an application showing their willingness to be admitted to bail. However, the grant of such "default bail" does not prohibit or otherwise prevent the subsequent arrest or re-arrest of the accused on cogent grounds for the same charge, after which the accused would be entitled to petition for regular bail to be considered on its own merit.
legal_tests_applied: When an application for bail is filed by an accused for enforcement of his indefeasible right alleged to have been accrued in his favour on account of default on the part of the investigating agency in completion of the investigation within the specified period, the Magistrate/court must dispose of it forthwith, on being satisfied that in fact the accused has been in custody for the period of 90 days or 60 days, as specified and no charge-sheet has been filed by the investigating agency.
why_appellant_lost: While the appellant succeeded in securing default bail (Issue 1), their implied position that this grant would prevent future arrest for the same charge was rejected. The court reasoned that default bail is a remedy for procedural delay, not a final adjudication on the merits, and therefore it would not prohibit or otherwise prevent the arrest or re-arrest of the accused on cogent grounds in respect of the charge in question.
why_respondent_won: While the respondent failed to prevent the grant of default bail (Issue 1), they succeeded on the principle that such a grant is not a permanent bar to custody (Issue 2). The court affirmed that the grant of default bail does not prohibit the subsequent arrest or re-arrest of the accused on cogent grounds, and upon such re-arrest, the accused must seek regular bail which will be considered on its own merit.
policy_considerations: An accused person should get a fair trial in accordance with the accepted principles of natural justice.
Every effort should be made to avoid delay in investigation and trial which is harmful not only to the individuals involved but also to society.

Such prompt action on the part of the Magistrate/court will not enable the prosecution to frustrate the object of the Act and the legislative mandate of an accused being released on bail on account of the default on the part of the investigating agency in completing the investigation within the period stipulated.
